This company built a data center floating in the Pacific Ocean.
They're called Pantelassa, and they might be pioneering a whole new category of data center technology.
See, a data center is really just thousands of computer chips that only need two things, electricity to think and water to cool.
On land, they compete with actual towns for both of those resources, which is why these projects keep getting blocked.
But the ocean has no towns, no permits, and no grids to constrain.
Of course, there is just one problem with an ocean-based data center.
There are no plugs to plug in for electricity.
So this floating data center was designed to make its own power.
Here's how it works.
Picture a giant floating lollipop in the sea with a round buoy on top and a long tube underneath.
Waves only move at the top of the surface, so underneath, it's actually very calm.
And that means the buoy rides up and down while the tube stays still.
Every wave that passes by squeezes seawater through its herbine.
Think of it like a bike pump, except the ocean waves is what's pushing the handle up and down.
That same seawater is also great for cooling the chips in the data center, so it accomplishes both tasks required.
Now, you'd think calm weather and no waves in the ocean would prevent this from running.
But it actually works a lot more like a battery.
The sun heats the air, the air makes wind, and the wind pushes the waves.
And those waves keep rolling long after the breeze stops.
So it's solar power that also works at night.
But there's just one more problem.
How do they get all that power back to the land to use?
And it turns out, they don't.
These things have no anchor, no fuel, and no cable to shore.
Instead, your AI query hits them, goes straight up to a satellite, and then goes straight back down to the data center.
The real problem making this tough is that the ocean typically destroys everything.
The salt eats metal, the barnacles grow out everything, and storms do what storms do.
And that's really the bet that Pantelassa's making, that they can figure out how to make this in a way the ocean can't destroy it.
The first full-size versions of this go live in the ocean later this year.
If they survive, your AI queries might start being powered by a floating data center in the ocean.

Scientists just figured out how to turn plastic bottles into cookies.
And these are real cookies that smell like vanilla and have protein and vitamins that humans can eat.
The technology behind this is called uBytes.
And the crazy part is NASA is actually paying for it.
So their astronauts can turn their own trash into food on the way to Mars.
It's pretty wild.
Now the way this whole thing works is actually pretty interesting.
Plastic and food are both made up of carbon molecules.
So first, scientists shred the plastic bottles and blast them with super hot, ultra high pressure water.
And this breaks them all the way down into molecules, basically a carbon soup.
Here's where it gets interesting.
They then feed that soup to a type of yeast.
This yeast is in the same family as the yeast that makes bread rise, except that this yeast is engineered to eat
Now, once the yeast eats the carbon molecules, what comes out the other side are protein, fats, and vitamins.
One strand of the yeast turns the carbon into vitamin A.
Another one makes the vanilla.
They then add fiber and sweetener and 3D print the mixture into cookies.
So what you're eating is not actually plastic, it's what the yeast made out of the plastic when it is made.
But the craziest part of this whole story is why NASA wants this technology in the first place.
See, a round trip to Mars will take approximately three years, and there's no way to pack three years' worth of food in a single spaceship.
So in theory, this method is a way that astronauts could turn their trash into edible food on the journey.
There's just one catch.
Nobody's ever taste tested these plastic cookies before.
The taste test is still waiting on FDA approval.
But if this works, there's a good chance the first cookie ever eaten on Mars will have been made out of plastic.
This is a prosthetic hand that runs on signals from your brain.
The company that invented this is called BrainCo, and they figured out something that most people don't know about losing a limb.
Even when your hand is gone, the brain never stops shooting nerve signals down your arm.
If you think about closing your fist, those neurons still fire, even though there's no fist to close.
Think of it like a TV remote with no TV.
The button still presses, but there's no TV to turn on.
So BrainCo built the receiver.
In their prosthetic, the sensors sit on your skin and receive those neural signals.
And an AI translates those into finger movements.
No surgery, no implant, no hardwired brain chip in your head.
And here's the part that makes this different.
Old prosthetics usually come with a rule book.
Flex this muscle to open, switch that muscle to close.
You had to be the one doing the learning to figure out how to use it.
Well now, with this prosthetic hand, it does the learning for you.
All you have to do is try to move like you used to, and the AI figures out what signals mean what movements.
Learning six different gestures only takes 10 minutes with this prosthetic,
And the more you use it, the easier it learns.
It's wild to say this, but we are entering a world where you can control prosthetics with your mind.

This is a brand new type of military aircraft from Andrew.
Its name is Thunder.
And the crazy part is that it can fly autonomously with no pilot and no cockpit.
Now, Thunder's job is like something straight out of Top Gun.
It flies right next to an Apache helicopter as its robotic wingman.
Think of it like the bodyguard flying shotgun, which takes the most dangerous job away so the crew doesn't have to.
But the coolest part about Thunder isn't that it flies autonomously, it's that it can fly in two different ways.
Thunder is what's called a tilt rail.
Which means the rotors can tilt forwards and backwards.
On takeoff, they point straight at the sky, so Thunder can lift off like a helicopter.
Then, once airborne, they tilt forward like propellers, so it can fly like a plane.
This single innovation is why Thunder can fly full speed with an Apache helicopter, while a normal drone would get left behind.

A soldier gives Thunder a task, and then it figures out the route, the formation, and the timing.
So the military is going from flying aircraft to coaching them.
Now, the Apache helicopter has been the king of attack aviation since the 1980s.
And Andrew says one Apache flying with three thunders can carry three times more weapons into a fight, while the crew can stay out of the most dangerous airspace.
It's early, but this feels like the beginning of the autonomous military era.

This is the cockpit of a brand new type of airplane, and almost everything you'd use to fly a normal plane is missing.
The yoke, the rubber pedals, even the trim wheel isn't here.
It's like sitting in a car that has no steering wheel to guide it.
And here's the craziest part.
To fly this plane, there's only one small stick.
That's it.
This plane is called the Skytron, and it was designed to eliminate all human pilot error.
It turns out around 80% of small plane crashes come down to pilot error, not broken parts.
And it's not because the pilots are bad, it's just that flying a plane requires the pilot to do so many things at once.
So Skytron's building a plane that helps prevent pilot mistakes.
If you pull the stick all the way back, the plane won't stall or fall out of the sky.
And if you point it at a mountain, it won't go.
And if you try to spin it erratically, it won't either.
There are three flight computers that vote on every action.
And if two outvote the one, it won't make the maneuver.
You also have two engines in this plane, so if one quits, the other can fly you home.
And of course, if everything fails, there's a parachute that pops that will safely lower the plane to the ground.
The goal of the Skytron plane is to make flying 99% autonomous.
You type in where you're going, it takes off, talks to air traffic control, and it lands.
The guy behind this project's name is Greg Mercer.
And he got into this because he sold a software company, started to learn to fly, and he hated how old planes felt.
So he's putting $20 million of his own money to try to reinvent small plane aviation.
Now, right now, Skytron is a wooden mock-up, but the first demo flight is scheduled for later this year.
And if it works, Greg might be spearheading a whole new category of aviation.
